title: Annotatio III §.XI (8) cont.: Wren — bread-substance flees at Hoc est corpus meum, leaving accidents behind
pass_a_gloss: Namely if we hear those to whom alone it is given to know these depths (Matthew Wren’s words in the Increpatio Bar Jesu, or Refutation of the Racovian Catechism p. 342): The Substance of Bread by no means passed into the Substance of the body, but terrified (as is fair) at those Divine words This is my body, so suddenly and utterly vanished that it did not even dare last long enough to pack its Accidents and carry the poor Species off with itself. How much less is it to be thought that the Substance of the Divine Body passed into that Bread-Substance which vanished?
pass_b_english: Wren (Increpatio Bar Jesu / Racovian Catechism refutation p. 342), on those who alone know these ‘depths’: bread-substance did not pass into body-substance.

Terrified at ‘This is my body,’ it vanished so fast it dared not even pack its accidents and drag the poor species along — still less did divine-body substance pass into that vanished bread-substance.
source_text: Scilicet, si istos audiamus, quibus solis datum est hæc βάθη callere (sunt verba Matthæi Wreni in Increpatione Bar Jesu, seu Refutatione Catechismi Racoviensis p. m. 342.) Substantia Panis neutiquam transiit in Substantiam corporis, sed exterrit a (ut par est,) ad Divina illa vocabula, Hoc est corpus meum, tam subito, prorsusque evanuit, ut nè durare quidem tantisper ausa fuerit, dum & Accidentia sua convasare, Speciesque misellas secum auferre posset. Quanto minus opinandum est, Substantiam Divini Corporis transiisse in eam, quæ evanuit, Panis Substantiam?
